title: Telling stories & real conversation
goal: Tell a story, report what people said, describe things with relative clauses, and sound natural with fillers, connectors and a few idioms.
intro: In this final unit you put everything together. Tamil has **no relative pronouns** ('who', 'which') — instead the verb itself becomes an adjective placed before the noun: **நான் வாங்கின புத்தகம்** 'the book I bought' (lit. 'I bought-which book'). You'll also master reported speech with **-ன்னு**, and the little words that make conversation flow: அப்புறம், அதாவது, சும்மா, பாவம்…

vocab.en: that is to say, I mean
just like that; as it is; on the way
oh dear! oh wow! (sympathy or surprise)
just; for no reason; for free

vocab.note: spoken: நியாபகம் nyābagam; ஞாபகம் இருக்கா? 'Do you remember?'

phrases.en: He said he'd come tomorrow. (lit. 'I'm coming' he said)
The film I saw yesterday was great.
Who's the boy standing over there?
I was just joking, don't be offended.
I mean, what I'm trying to say is…
Every town is my town, everyone is my kin. (2,000-year-old Sangam verse)

grammar.title: Relative clauses: the adjectival participle
grammar.body:
Tamil turns a whole clause into an adjective by putting the verb in its **relative-participle** form and placing it **before** the noun:

**Past**: past stem + **-அ** — வாங்கின *vāngina* 'that (someone) bought', வந்த *vanda* 'that came', பாத்த *pātta* 'that (someone) saw', சொன்ன *sonna* 'that (someone) said'
**Present**: present stem + **-அ** — வர்ற *varra* 'that comes / is coming', படிக்கிற *paḍikkira* 'that studies'
**Future/habitual**: **-உம்** — வரும் *varum* 'that will come', இருக்கும் 'that will be'
**Negative**: **-ஆத** — வராத *varāda* 'that doesn't/didn't come', தெரியாத 'unknown'

The participle doesn't change for person, and there's no 'who/which': **நேத்து வந்த ஆளு** 'the person who came yesterday', **நான் படிக்கிற புத்தகம்** 'the book I'm reading', **தமிழ் தெரியாத வெளிநாட்டுக்காரர்** 'a foreigner who doesn't know Tamil'. Add **-து** to make a noun 'the one that…' / 'the fact that…': நீங்க சொன்னது 'what you said'.

examples.en: my elder sister who lives in Chennai
The boy who phoned yesterday has come.
There's no food I don't like.

grammar.title: Reported speech with -ன்னு
grammar.body:
Tamil prefers **direct** quotation. You repeat what someone said in their own words, close it with **-ன்னு** *-nnu* (written என்று), then add the speech verb: **அவன் 'வர்றேன்'னு சொன்னான்** → அவன் வர்றேன்னு சொன்னான் 'He said he'd come' (lit. 'I'm coming,' he said).

Note that the inner verb keeps the original speaker's person: அவரு வர்றேன்னு சொன்னாரு (with *I*-ending) = 'he said that he would come'. If you say அவரு வருவாருன்னு சொன்னாரு instead, it normally means he said that some *other* man would come.

**Commands** are reported with the infinitive + **சொல்லு**: என்னை வரச் சொன்னாங்க 'they told me to come'. **Questions** keep their form: வர்றீங்களான்னு கேட்டாங்க 'they asked if you're coming'. -ன்னு also names things: இதுக்குத் தமிழ்ல என்னன்னு சொல்லுவாங்க? 'What is this called in Tamil?'

examples.en: What do you call this in Tamil?
I heard that tomorrow is a holiday.

grammar.title: Sounding natural: connectors, fillers and the -தான் / -உம் / -ஏ particles
grammar.body:
Real conversation is held together by small words:

**அப்புறம்** 'and then; so…' · **அதனால** 'so' · **ஆனா** 'but' · **இருந்தாலும்** 'even so' · **கடைசில** 'in the end' · **அதாவது** 'I mean' · **சொல்லப்போனா** 'actually' · **சும்மா** 'just' · **பாவம்** 'poor thing' · **அடடா / ஐயோ** (sympathy) · **அப்படியா?** 'really?' · **ஆமா ஆமா** 'yes, yes (I'm listening)'

Three particles add nuance to any word: **-தான்** *-dān* 'it's precisely…, only' (நான்தான் 'it was me'), **-உம்** *-um* 'also, too; and' (நானும் 'me too'; அவனும் அவளும் 'he and she'), and **-ஏ** *-ē* emphasis 'the very…' (இப்போவே 'right now').

examples.en: It was me who said it.
It's hard, sure, but we'll try anyway.

dialogue.title: The story of the lost tourist
dialogue.setting: Karthik tells Priya a funny story over tea at a roadside stall.

lines.speaker: Karthik
lines.native: தெரியுமா, நேத்து ஒரு வேடிக்கையான விஷயம் நடந்துச்சு.
lines.roman: teriyumā, nēttu oru vēḍikkaiyāna vishayam naḍanducchu.
lines.en: You know, something funny happened yesterday.

lines.speaker: Karthik
lines.native: பீச்சுல ஒரு வெளிநாட்டுக்காரர் என்கிட்ட வந்து, சுத்தமான தமிழ்ல வழி கேட்டாரு.
lines.roman: bīcchula oru veḷināṭṭukkārar enkiṭṭa vandu, suttamāna tamiḻla vaḻi kēṭṭāru.
lines.en: At the beach a foreigner came up to me and asked the way in pure Tamil.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.en: Wow! Did he speak Tamil well?

lines.speaker: Karthik
lines.native: ரொம்ப நல்லா! ஆனா புத்தகத்துல இருக்கிற மாதிரி பேசினாரு. 'தாங்கள் எங்கே செல்கிறீர்கள்?'னு கேட்டாரு!
lines.roman: romba nallā! ānā puttagattula irukkira mādiri pēsināru. 'tāngaḷ engē selgirīrgaḷ?'nu kēṭṭāru!
lines.en: Very well! But he talked like a book. He asked, 'Whither art thou proceeding?'

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.native: ஹா ஹா! அப்புறம் நீ என்ன சொன்ன?
lines.roman: hā hā! appuram nī enna sonna?
lines.en: Ha ha! Then what did you say?

lines.speaker: Karthik
lines.native: நான் சிரிச்சுட்டேன். அப்புறம் 'எங்க போகணும் சார்?'னு கேட்டேன்.
lines.roman: nān siricchuṭṭēn. appuram 'enga pōgaṇum sār?'nu kēṭṭēn.
lines.en: I burst out laughing. Then I asked, 'Where d'you need to go, sir?'

lines.speaker: Karthik
lines.en: No! He said, 'I haven't learned spoken Tamil yet.'

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.native: இருந்தாலும் பெரிய விஷயம்தான். கடைசில அவரு எங்க போனாரு?
lines.roman: irundālum periya vishayamdān. kaḍaisila avaru enga pōnāru?
lines.en: Still, that's quite something. Where did he go in the end?

lines.speaker: Karthik
lines.native: நானே அவரைக் கூட்டிட்டுப் போனேன். இப்போ அவரு என் ஃப்ரெண்ட்!
lines.roman: nānē avaraik kūṭṭiṭṭup pōnēn. ippō avaru en freṇḍ!
lines.en: I took him there myself. Now he's my friend!

culture: The line **யாதும் ஊரே யாவரும் கேளிர்** 'every town is my town, everyone is my kin', from the Sangam poet Kaniyan Pungundranar, is one of the most quoted lines in Tamil — it has even been cited at the United Nations. Tamils love wordplay, proverbs (பழமொழி) and film dialogue quotes in conversation. And as Karthik's story shows, the best compliment a learner can get is to be told they speak like a real person, not a book — so keep practising your பேச்சுத் தமிழ்!
